groups.high: Reasonable accommodation under Articles 2 and 5 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities means necessary and appropriate modifications in a particular case that do not impose a disproportionate or undue burden, enabling equal enjoyment of rights. Denial is a form of disability discrimination. Unlike general accessibility, which addresses barriers in advance for groups, accommodation responds to an individual's circumstances; both obligations matter. Identify the barrier with the person rather than assuming a diagnosis determines the solution. Options include flexible scheduling, adapted equipment, remote work where effective, sign-language interpretation, accessible premises, and Braille, large-print, or accessible digital information. Assess whether the adjustment actually enables equal participation and whether alternatives are equally effective. Burden assessment should consider relevant resources, cost, available support, and organizational circumstances, not simply inconvenience or preference. A large organization cannot assess affordability solely by a tiny departmental budget without considering the relevant context. Consultation matters, but lack of agreement does not automatically extinguish the duty. Employers and service providers have responsibilities through the state's equality framework; precise procedures and remedies depend on applicable law. Accommodation is not a special favor or a guarantee of every requested adjustment. It is a means of removing a specific barrier without imposing an undue burden, while respecting the person's dignity and choices.
groups.mid: CRPD stands for the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Reasonable accommodation is a necessary, suitable adjustment for an individual with a disability. It must not impose a disproportionate or undue burden. Articles 2 and 5 of the CRPD define the term. Denial constitutes disability discrimination. Accessibility removes barriers in advance for groups. Accommodation responds to one person's case. Both matter. Talk with the person about the barrier. Do not pick a solution from a diagnosis alone. Examples include flexible hours, adapted tools, working from home where useful, a sign-language interpreter, usable premises, and Braille, large-print, or accessible digital text. Check that a change lets the person take part equally. Another option may work just as well. A burden assessment looks at cost, relevant resources, support, and the organization's situation. Inconvenience or the provider's preference is not enough. A large provider may need to consider more than one team's budget. Consultation matters, but disagreement does not simply erase the duty. Employers and services have duties under the relevant equality law. That law sets procedures and remedies. This is not a favor or a promise of every requested change. It removes a real barrier while respecting dignity and choice.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Some people need a change to use a service or do a job on equal terms. This is reasonable accommodation. Articles 2 and 5 of the CRPD protect it. The change must be needed and suitable. It must not impose a disproportionate or undue burden. That is an excessive burden, not just something a provider does not like. Denial is a form of discrimination. This means refusing a needed change can be unfair treatment. Accessibility removes barriers in advance for groups. A barrier is something that gets in the way of taking part. This change meets one person's needs in a particular case. Both matter. Ask the person what gets in the way. Do not guess from a diagnosis. A change might be different hours, adapted tools, or working from home if that works. It might be a sign-language interpreter, an entrance they can use, or Braille, large print, or digital text. Check that it really helps. Another option may work just as well. Check cost, resources, support, and the whole situation. Mere inconvenience is not enough to show undue burden. The funds may be more than one small team's budget. Talk through the options. Failure to agree does not end the duty. Local equality law sets duties, steps, and remedies for employers and services. This is not a favor or a promise of every request. It is about removing a real barrier fairly and respecting choice.
groups.source_review: CRPD Articles2/5 definition and denial-as-discrimination framework checked via UN treaty materials; examples are illustrative, not guaranteed outcomes.
groups.notes: Clarified accessibility/accommodation distinction and that provider disagreement does not itself erase duty. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 12 of the CRPD affirms recognition as a person before the law and equal legal capacity in all aspects of life. Legal capacity concerns holding and exercising rights, not a diagnostic label or performance on a cognitive test. States must provide access to the support a person may need in exercising it. Support can include accessible information, communication assistance, trusted decision supporters, and independent advice. It must respect the person's rights, will, and preferences rather than substitute a supporter’s preferred outcome. Safeguards must prevent abuse, conflict of interest, and undue influence; be proportionate and tailored; operate for the shortest possible time; and undergo regular review by a competent independent authority. Article 12 also protects ownership and inheritance, control of financial affairs, and equal access to credit, with protection against arbitrary deprivation of property. The CRPD Committee's General Comment No. 1 calls for replacing substitute decision-making with supported decision-making. A claim that guardianship is automatically compatible if called a last resort misstates that interpretation. When preferences remain unclear despite significant efforts, the Committee favors the best interpretation of will and preferences, not an adult best-interests substitute. National laws and practices still vary and may not fully comply; describe that as an implementation issue, not as removal of the Convention right.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 12 of the CRPD protects equal legal capacity. This means being a person before the law, holding rights, and being able to use them. A diagnosis or a score on a thinking test does not by itself remove the right. States must give access to needed support. It can mean plain information, communication help, a trusted supporter, or independent advice. Support must respect the person's rights, will, and preferences. It should help them decide, not replace their choice. Safeguards must prevent abuse, conflicts of interest, and undue influence. They must fit the person, last the shortest possible time, and be reviewed regularly by a skilled independent body. The article also covers owning and inheriting property, managing money, and equal access to credit. It guards against arbitrary loss of property. The CRPD Committee explains the right in General Comment No. 1. It calls for supported decisions instead of substitute decisions. Calling guardianship a last resort does not make it comply with that view. If the person's wishes remain unclear despite real efforts, seek the best interpretation of their will and preferences. Do not simply choose what someone else thinks is in an adult's best interests. National laws still differ and some fall short. The right is not erased by that failure.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 12 of the CRPD says people with disabilities have equal legal capacity. They have rights and can use them. For example, they should be able to make a choice, not have someone take over just because they need help. They are persons before the law. A diagnosis or thinking test does not by itself take this away. Some people need help to choose or speak. States must give access to that support. Help may be clear text, a way to communicate, a trusted person, or independent advice. It must respect your rights and what you want. Your will and preferences matter. It should support your choice, not replace it. Rules must guard against abuse and undue influence. A helper must not pressure you or put their interests first. Safeguards must fit your case and last as briefly as possible. A skilled independent body must check them regularly. The review must be real, not a rubber stamp. It must be able to judge the case, not just accept what a helper says. Article 12 also protects owning and inheriting property, managing money, and equal access to loans. Property must not be taken without a sound legal basis. General Comment No. 1 explains the CRPD Committee's view. This is the group that explains what the treaty means. It calls for support, not takeover of decisions. Calling takeover a last resort does not make it right under that view. Your wishes may stay unclear after real efforts. Then seek the best reading of your will and preferences. Do not just choose what others think is best for you. Local laws may fall short. The right still matters.
groups.source_review: Article12 safeguards and Committee interpretation checked against UN/WHO-OHCHR materials.
groups.notes: Corrected claim last-resort substitute guardianship is endorsed as treaty-compliant. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 14 of the CRPD guarantees liberty and security on an equal basis with others. Persons with disabilities must not be deprived of liberty unlawfully or arbitrarily; any deprivation must conform to law, and disability must never itself justify it. A disability diagnosis, a need for support, or an assumption of incapacity is not a sufficient basis for confinement. The CRPD Committee interprets this protection against disability-based detention, including schemes combining impairment with additional criteria. Describing a less restrictive disability-based detention as automatically compliant would therefore be misleading. If a person with a disability is deprived of liberty through a lawful process, they retain the human-rights guarantees applicable to others and must be treated consistently with the Convention, including reasonable accommodation. Accessible information, communication assistance, legal help, and an effective means of challenging detention can make those guarantees practical. Custodial conditions must not expose someone to neglect, abuse, or inaccessible essential care. Article 12's equal legal capacity should not be replaced by a blanket disability-based incapacity presumption. Independent review and remedies arise within the wider applicable human-rights framework; Article 14 is not a license to confine merely because a review is offered. States should remove disability-based barriers and provide support in the community rather than equating support needs with loss of freedom.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 14 of the CRPD protects liberty and security on equal terms. Detention must not be unlawful or arbitrary. Disability must never itself justify loss of liberty. A diagnosis is not enough to confine someone. Nor is a need for support or a belief they cannot decide. The CRPD Committee also rejects schemes using disability plus extra criteria to allow detention. A less restrictive setting does not automatically make this lawful. If a person is detained through a lawful process, they keep the same human-rights safeguards as others. Treatment must follow the Convention, including reasonable accommodation. This may require usable information and communication help. Legal advice and a real way to challenge detention matter too. Conditions must guard against neglect and abuse. Essential care must be accessible. Article 12 also protects equal legal capacity. It must not be replaced by a blanket rule that disability makes someone incapable. Independent review and remedies matter. These come under the wider human-rights framework. But review alone is not permission to confine someone because of disability. States should remove barriers and provide support in the community. Needing help is not the same as losing freedom.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 14 of the CRPD protects liberty and security on equal terms. No detention may be unlawful or arbitrary. Disability must never itself justify taking freedom away. A diagnosis is not enough. Nor is a need for support or a belief that someone cannot decide. The CRPD Committee rejects detention based on disability plus extra criteria too. A less restrictive place does not make that lawful by itself. Someone held through a lawful process keeps the same human-rights safeguards as others. Treatment must follow the Convention. It must include reasonable accommodation. That can mean usable text, help to communicate, legal advice, and a real way to challenge detention. Conditions must guard against neglect and abuse. Essential care must be accessible. Article 12 protects equal legal capacity. A blanket rule that disability makes a person incapable is not a substitute. Independent review and remedies matter under other human-rights rules. Review alone is not permission to confine a person because of disability. States should remove barriers and offer support in the community. Needing help is not the same as losing freedom.
groups.source_review: Article14 treaty rule and Committee/WHO-OHCHR supported-community approach checked; broader procedural rights distinguished from exact article wording.
groups.notes: Removed claim individualized incapacity assessments justify detention and automatic least-restrictive compliance. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 15 of the CRPD prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. It specifically forbids medical or scientific experimentation without free consent. States must take effective legislative, administrative, judicial, and other measures to prevent such treatment on an equal basis with others. The prohibition cannot be suspended merely by invoking war, emergency, disability, or a purported therapeutic benefit. Genuine consent requires understandable information, freedom from coercion, and respect for the person's decision; accessible communication and decision support may be needed. A diagnosis does not make a person available for involuntary experimentation. Abusive restraint, forced sterilization, severe neglect, or coercive interventions can raise serious issues under Article 15 and related rights; the legal characterization depends on the facts and must not be reduced to the label treatment. Prevention includes oversight, accessible complaint routes, investigation, accountability, and effective remedies under the applicable legal framework. Article 13 supports access to justice and procedural accommodations; Articles 17 and 25 address integrity and health-related consent. Article 15 does not state a universal reversal of the criminal burden of proof, nor should every clinical error be automatically labeled torture without legal analysis. The central point is equal protection of dignity and bodily integrity, with active prevention of abuse rather than a blanket medical-authority exception.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 15 of the CRPD bans torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. It bans medical or scientific experiments without free consent. States must use effective laws, courts, administration, and other steps to prevent it. War, an emergency, disability, or a claim of health benefit does not suspend the ban. Consent must be a real choice. No one should be pressured. People need information they can understand. They may need help to communicate or decide. A diagnosis does not allow experiments against a person's will. Abusive restraint, forced sterilization, severe neglect, and coercive care can raise serious rights issues. The facts and law matter. Calling it treatment does not make abuse acceptable. States need oversight and safe complaint routes. They need proper inquiry, accountability, and remedies under the relevant law. Article 13 supports access to justice and help with legal procedures. Articles 17 and 25 concern personal integrity and consent in health care. Article 15 does not reverse the criminal burden of proof in every case. Nor is every medical error automatically torture. The goal is equal protection of dignity and the body, with practical action to prevent abuse.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 15 of the CRPD bans torture. It bans cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment too. It also bans medical or scientific experiments without free consent. That means a real yes, not one forced from a person. States must prevent this with effective laws and courts. They must use administration and other steps too. War does not cancel the ban. Nor does an emergency, disability, or a claim that abuse helps health. Free consent is a real choice with no pressure. Explain the facts in a form the person can use. They may need help to speak or decide. A diagnosis does not allow experiments against their will. Abusive restraints can raise serious rights issues. So can forced sterilization, severe neglect, and forced care. Restraints hold or tie a person in place. Sterilization means making someone unable to have children. Check the facts and law. Calling abuse treatment does not make it right. People need safe ways to complain. States need oversight and proper inquiry. They need accountability and remedies too. This means checking what happened, holding those at fault to account, and providing redress. Article 13 covers access to justice and help in legal procedures. Articles 17 and 25 cover personal integrity and health-care consent. They concern respect for your body and mind, and your say in care. Article 15 does not change all criminal proof rules. Not every medical error is torture. The goal is equal dignity and bodily protection. Real steps must prevent abuse. A medical label does not make an act right. It must respect these rights.
groups.source_review: Article15 consent and prevention rule checked; related13/17/25 distinguished; no categorical classification of all malpractice as torture.
groups.notes: Corrected incomplete state-measures list and invented general reversal of burden of proof. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 22 of the CRPD protects privacy for persons with disabilities regardless of residence or living arrangements. It prohibits arbitrary or unlawful interference with privacy, family, home, correspondence, and other communications, as well as unlawful attacks on honor and reputation. The person is entitled to legal protection against such interference or attacks. States must protect the privacy of personal, health, and rehabilitation information on an equal basis with others. Living in a care facility, receiving support, or having a diagnosis does not erase confidentiality or authorize routine exposure of private records. Providers should use lawful, proportionate information practices and safeguards against unauthorized disclosure, while respecting the person's involvement and choices. Consent and accessible explanations are important, but Article 22 should not be presented as prohibiting every form of legally justified processing without consent; applicable law may supply other narrowly governed bases. Equal protection is a floor, not a ban on additional safeguards where heightened risks justify them. A hospital may therefore need tailored security or communication arrangements without imposing inferior rights. State duties include an effective legal framework and protection against public and private misuse, with complaint and remedy routes under applicable law. Privacy is not limited to medical files: family relationships, the home, private messages, and reputation also require protection. Practical assistance should preserve autonomy rather than become a reason for surveillance.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 22 of the CRPD protects privacy wherever a person lives. It bars arbitrary or unlawful intrusion into private life, family, home, mail, and other messages. It also bars unlawful attacks on honor and reputation. People have a right to legal protection. States must protect personal, health, and rehabilitation information on equal terms. A care home, support needs, or a diagnosis does not remove that right. Staff must keep records safe and share them on a lawful, proportionate basis. Consent and usable explanations matter. But consent is not the only legal ground for every use of data. Other lawful grounds need proper safeguards. Equal protection does not ban extra safety measures where risks are greater. A hospital may need tailored security or a safer way to contact a patient. That should strengthen rights, not reduce them. States need laws and complaint and remedy routes for misuse by public and private bodies. The right is not just about medical files. It covers family, home, messages, and reputation. Help must respect choice rather than become an excuse for surveillance.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Your disability does not take away privacy. Article 22 of the CRPD protects it wherever you live. That includes a care home. There must be no arbitrary or unlawful intrusion into your private life, family, home, mail, or messages. There must be no unlawful attack on your honor or reputation. You have a right to legal protection. Personal, health, and rehabilitation records need equal privacy protection. Needing help does not let staff show records to anyone they choose. Sharing needs a lawful, proportionate basis and safeguards. Consent and clear explanations matter. But consent is not the only legal ground for every use of data. Other lawful grounds still need safeguards. Equal rights do not forbid extra protection where risk is high. A hospital may need safer storage or private ways to contact you. This should improve rights, not reduce them. States need laws and ways to complain and seek a remedy for misuse by public or private bodies. Privacy is more than medical files. It also protects your family life, home, messages, and reputation. Help should respect choice, not become an excuse for surveillance.
groups.source_review: Article22 complete scope including regardless of living arrangements checked; general lawful-processing caveat avoids unsupported absolute consent rule.
groups.notes: Corrected claim equal protection forbids stronger safeguards or any nonconsensual lawful processing. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 24 of the CRPD requires an inclusive education system at all levels and lifelong learning, directed toward dignity, self-worth, human potential, talents, creativity, and participation in a free society. Inclusion is more than placing a learner in an unchanged mainstream classroom: the system must remove barriers to effective participation. Persons with disabilities must not be excluded from the general education system on disability grounds, and children must not be excluded from free compulsory primary or secondary education on that basis. States must ensure access to inclusive, quality, free primary and secondary education in the communities where learners live, reasonable accommodation, support within the general system, and effective individualized support consistent with full inclusion. Accessible materials, assistive technology, Braille, sign language, and appropriate communication methods can be essential. Teachers and staff need training, and the linguistic identity of the deaf community must be respected. General tertiary education, vocational training, adult education, and lifelong learning must also be accessible without discrimination and with reasonable accommodation. Universal design can reduce barriers in advance but does not eliminate individual adjustments. Do not equate inclusion with mere integration, or assert that every favored curriculum reform is expressly mandated by the article. The standard concerns meaningful learning and participation, not simply enrollment numbers or charity.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 24 of the CRPD protects inclusive education at every level and through life. It should develop dignity and potential. It should develop talents, creativity, and a place in society. Inclusion is not just a seat in an unchanged class. Disability must not exclude someone from the general system. It must not keep a child out of free compulsory primary or secondary school. States must provide inclusive, quality, free primary and secondary education. Learners need access in the communities where they live. They must provide reasonable accommodation and support in the general system. Help must fit the learner and support full inclusion. Books may need a usable format. Braille and sign language may be needed. So may assistive technology or other ways to communicate. Teachers and staff need training. The deaf community's language identity matters. College and job training must be open on equal terms. So must adult study and learning through life. There must be no discrimination. Reasonable accommodation is required there too. Design that fits many needs can remove barriers early. Some learners still need changes for their own case. Inclusion is not mere integration. Integration may just fit a learner into a system that refuses to change. Article 24 does not list every possible curriculum reform as a duty. Real learning and taking part matter, not just enrollment.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 24 of the CRPD is about inclusive education. It covers every level and learning through life. The aim is dignity, potential, talents, creativity, and taking part in society. A seat in a class is not enough if barriers still block learning. Disability must not keep a person out of the general system. It must not bar a child from free compulsory primary or secondary school. States must provide inclusive, quality, free primary and secondary education where learners live. They must give reasonable accommodation. This means needed changes for the learner's case. Support must be in the general system and help full inclusion. Books may need a form the learner can use. Braille or sign language may be needed. So may assistive technology or other ways to communicate. Teachers and staff need training. Deaf learners' language identity matters. College, job training, adult study, and learning through life must be open on equal terms. Disability must not mean worse treatment. Reasonable accommodation is needed there too. Good design can remove barriers for many people. Some still need individual changes. Inclusion is not just fitting into a school that will not change. Article 24 does not require every possible curriculum reform. The aim is real learning and taking part, not just enrollment.
groups.source_review: Article24 school exclusion, support, communication and lifelong education terms checked.
groups.notes: Corrected integration/inclusion conflation and unsupported curriculum-decolonization-as-express-duty claim. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 26 of the CRPD requires effective measures enabling maximum independence, physical, mental, social, and vocational ability, and full inclusion. Habilitation commonly develops skills not previously acquired; rehabilitation commonly restores or supports functions affected by illness, injury, or other change. Services extend beyond clinical treatment to health, employment, education, and social services, with peer support where appropriate. States must organize, strengthen, and extend comprehensive programs beginning at the earliest possible stage, based on multidisciplinary assessment of individual needs and strengths. They must support community participation, be voluntary, and be available as close as possible to people's communities, including rural areas. Early intervention does not justify compulsory treatment or an assumption that adults cannot benefit. The article promotes initial and continuing staff training and the availability, knowledge, and use of assistive devices and technologies. Coordination across services helps skills translate into everyday autonomy and participation. The text does not prescribe a universal newborn screening program or a fixed neuroplasticity deadline, and it should not be paraphrased as an automatic promise of every requested service regardless of context. Nor should success be measured solely by clinical correction. Choice, accessibility, relevant support, and participation in ordinary community life are central to a rights-based approach.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Habilitation helps people gain skills not learned before. Rehabilitation helps restore or support abilities affected by illness, injury, or change. Article 26 of the CRPD covers both. The goal is maximum independence, ability, and full inclusion in society. Help goes beyond a clinic. It covers health, work, education, and social services, with peer support where appropriate. States must build and strengthen broad services. They should start as early as possible. Staff from different fields should assess the person's needs and strengths. Services must be voluntary and help people take part in community life. They should be as close to home as possible, including in rural areas. Early help does not mean forced treatment or that adults cannot benefit. Staff need training at the start and throughout their work. States should promote assistive devices and technology and explain their use. Services should work together so skills help in daily life. The article does not require one newborn screening system or set a fixed age when learning stops. It does not promise every requested service in all cases. Success includes choice, access, useful support, and taking part, not only a better clinical result.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Habilitation helps people learn skills they did not have before. Rehabilitation helps restore or support abilities affected by illness, injury, or change. Article 26 of the CRPD covers both. The aim is more independence, ability, and full inclusion in society. Help is not only medical care. It can involve health, work, education, social services, and peer support. States must organize and strengthen broad services. They should start as early as possible. Different professionals should assess the person's needs and strengths. The person must be free to choose these services. They should help people take part in community life. They should be as close to home as possible, including in rural places. Early help is not a reason to force treatment. It does not mean adults are too late to learn. Staff need training at the start and as they continue working. States should promote useful assistive devices and technology and explain how to use them. Services should work together so skills help in daily life. The article does not require one screening program for all newborns. It gives no fixed age when learning must stop. It does not promise every service a person requests. Success is more than a better clinical test. Choice, access, practical help, and taking part in the community all matter.
groups.source_review: Article26 voluntariness, early multidisciplinary assessment, rural provision, training and technology checked.
groups.notes: Removed universal infant screening and fixed neuroplasticity-window claims; retained voluntary community basis. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 27 of the CRPD recognizes the right to work on an equal basis with others, including the opportunity to earn a living through freely chosen or accepted work in an open, inclusive, accessible labor market. States must prohibit disability discrimination in recruitment, hiring, continued employment, advancement, and safe and healthy working conditions. Protections include equal opportunity and remuneration for work of equal value, protection from harassment, and grievance redress. Reasonable accommodation in the workplace is required; necessary appropriate adjustments are assessed without disproportionate or undue burden under the Convention's definition. States must support access to vocational guidance, placement, training, job retention, return to work, and rehabilitation. They must employ persons with disabilities in the public sector and promote private-sector employment through appropriate policies, including possible incentives or affirmative action. Self-employment, entrepreneurship, cooperatives, and starting a business must also be promoted. Persons with disabilities must be able to exercise labor and trade-union rights equally and must not be held in slavery, servitude, or forced labor. These are duties to secure fair opportunity and remove barriers, not a guarantee of a particular job or an identical financial subsidy for every applicant. Accessible recruitment, suitable adjustments, effective complaints, and inclusive ordinary workplaces make the right practical rather than confining people to segregated options.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 27 of the CRPD protects equal rights at work. People should earn a living through work they freely choose or accept. The job market should be open, inclusive, and accessible. States must ban disability discrimination in hiring, keeping a job, promotion, and safe working conditions. Rights include equal chances and equal pay for work of equal value. They include no harassment and a way to raise grievances. Workplaces must provide reasonable accommodation. This means needed, suitable changes without a disproportionate or undue burden. States must support job advice, training, placement, keeping work, return to work, and rehabilitation. They must employ people with disabilities in public jobs and promote private-sector work. Tools may include incentives and affirmative action. They must also promote self-employment, starting businesses, and cooperatives. People have equal labor and trade-union rights. They must not face slavery, servitude, or forced labor. This is not a promise of a particular job or the same grant for all. The aim is fair opportunity and removing barriers. Usable hiring, effective workplace changes, real complaint routes, and ordinary inclusive workplaces make the right practical.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 27 of the CRPD protects equal rights at work. Work should be freely chosen or accepted. The job market should be open, inclusive, and accessible. Disability must not cause discrimination in hiring, keeping a job, promotion, or safe work. Rights include equal chances, equal pay for work of equal value, no harassment, and a way to complain. Workplaces must provide reasonable accommodation. This means needed, suitable changes without a disproportionate or undue burden. States must support job advice, skills, placement, keeping jobs, and return to work. Rehabilitation can help. States must hire people with disabilities in public jobs and promote private-sector work. Incentives or affirmative action can help. They must also promote self-employment, businesses, and cooperatives. Workers have equal labor rights. Their trade-union rights are equal too. They must not face slavery, servitude, or forced labor. The treaty does not promise one specific job or the same grant for all. It requires fair opportunity and removal of barriers. Usable hiring, effective changes at work, and real complaint routes help make the right work in ordinary workplaces.
groups.source_review: Article27 employment lifecycle, public/private sector, self-employment and forced-labor clauses checked.
groups.notes: Clarified no unconditional individualized financial-support or guaranteed-job entitlement. Root reviewed and revised plain-language prose for FK bounds without changing the source-corrected brief.

groups.high: Article 28, not Article 25, of the CRPD recognizes an adequate standard of living for persons with disabilities and their families, including adequate food, clothing, housing, and continuous improvement of living conditions. States must take appropriate steps to realize this right without disability discrimination. Social protection includes equal access to clean water; affordable disability-related services, devices, and assistance; poverty-reduction and social-protection programs, particularly for women, girls, and older persons with disabilities; assistance with disability-related expenses for families living in poverty, including training, counseling, financial help, and respite care; access to public housing; and equal access to retirement benefits. Article 19's community-living rights, Article 24's education rights, Article 25's health rights, and Article 27's work rights reinforce but do not replace this provision. Accessible housing and services must support choice rather than require institutional residence as the price of assistance. Economic and social rights involve progressive realization using maximum available resources under Article 4(2), while discrimination must not be excused as a future budgetary issue. Respecting rights, protecting against private abuse, and taking effective public measures all matter. The article does not guarantee identical incomes or instant provision of any chosen home. It requires an adequate, inclusive standard and practical steps addressing poverty and disability-related barriers.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 28 of the CRPD protects a decent standard of living. It covers people with disabilities and their families. It includes adequate food, clothes, housing, and better living conditions over time. Article 25 is about health. States must act without unfair treatment because of disability. People need equal access to clean water. Devices and services should be at a price they can pay. So should help for disability needs. They need access to social protection and poverty programs. Women, girls, and older people need special attention. Families in poverty need help with extra disability costs. Help can include training and counseling. It can include money and respite care. Respite care gives a caregiver a break. People need access to public housing. They need equal access to retirement benefits too. Article 19 supports life in the community. Articles 24, 25, and 27 cover school, health, and work. Help must not force people into an institution. Article 4(2) lets some economic and social rights improve in stages. States must use all the resources available. They cannot put off the ban on unfair treatment. They must respect rights and guard against private abuse. They must act too. It is not a promise of equal incomes or any chosen home at once. It calls for a decent life and real work on poverty and barriers.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 28 of the CRPD protects a decent life. It covers people with disabilities. It covers their families too. The rights belong to them wherever they live. They are not just for people in a care home. They need enough food, clothes, and housing. Living conditions should keep getting better. Article 25 is about health. A state must not treat people worse because of disability. They need equal access to clean water. Devices and services should be at a price they can pay. So should help for needs linked to disability. They need access to social protection. They need programs to reduce poverty. Social protection means support when people need it, not just pay from a job. Women and girls need special attention. Older people do too. Poor families need help with extra costs linked to these needs. Help can be training or counseling. Counseling can mean talking with a person who helps you work through problems. It can be money or respite care. Respite care gives a caregiver a break. Public housing must be open to them. It means homes provided through a public program. They also need equal access to retirement benefits. These are benefits for old age. People must have an equal chance to receive them. Their disability must not shut them out. Article 19 supports life in the community. Articles 24, 25, and 27 cover school, health, and work. Help must not force people into an institution. Article 4(2) allows some rights to improve in stages. These are economic and social rights. States must use the most resources available. This means doing as much as they can with what they have. It does not mean doing nothing. They cannot just delay equal treatment. They must respect rights. They must guard against private abuse. They must act. The rule does not promise the same income for all. It does not promise any chosen house at once. The aim is a decent life and real steps on poverty and barriers. The cost of a device or needed help can make life harder. This can be true even if a family has some income.

groups.high: Article 29 of the CRPD requires equal political rights and opportunities for persons with disabilities, including voting, election, holding office, and public functions. Voting procedures, facilities, and materials must be appropriate, accessible, and easy to understand and use. Secret ballots in elections and public referendums must be protected against intimidation. The voter’s own will must determine the choice; assistance is not permission for family, officials, or supporters to substitute theirs. Where necessary and requested, a voter must be allowed assistance by a person of their own choice. Assistive and new technologies should be facilitated where appropriate, but the article does not mandate internet voting, eye-tracking, or a particular remote platform in every election. Physical access, understandable information, accessible ballot design, and staff training can be as important as digital tools. Public participation extends beyond election day: states must promote an environment for involvement in public affairs, political parties, nongovernmental associations, and organizations representing persons with disabilities at local, national, regional, and international levels. Accessibility and privacy should reinforce each other rather than using secrecy to prohibit requested assistance. The aim is effective participation on an equal basis, not merely formal possession of a vote that inaccessible procedures prevent someone from casting.
groups.mid: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 29 of the CRPD protects equal political rights. People with disabilities can vote and stand for election. They can hold office and perform public roles too. Voting places, steps, and materials must be accessible and easy to understand and use. Elections and public referendums need secret ballots without intimidation. The voter's own choice must decide the vote. Family, officials, and helpers must not choose for them. If help is needed and requested, the voter must be allowed a person of their own choice. Assistive technology can help where appropriate. The article does not require internet voting, eye-tracking, or one remote system in every election. A usable entrance, clear text, a suitable ballot, and trained staff also matter. States must support public affairs, parties, civic groups, and organizations of people with disabilities. This includes local, national, regional, and international levels. A secret vote must not be an excuse to ban requested help. Access and privacy should work together. The goal is a right people can use, not a vote blocked by the process.
groups.low: CRPD is the UN treaty on the rights of persons with disabilities. Article 29 of the CRPD protects political rights. People with disabilities can vote. They can stand for election. They can hold office and do public roles on equal terms. Voting places and materials must be easy to reach and use. The steps must be clear. Votes in elections and public referendums must be secret. A public referendum lets people vote on a public question. It is not just a vote to choose a person for office. No one should frighten or pressure a voter. It must be their own choice. A helper, relative, or official must not choose for them. A voter who needs help and asks for it can choose who assists. Useful assistive technology should be supported where it fits. It is a tool that helps a person do a task. But not every election must use internet voting. It need not use eye-tracking or one remote system either. A usable entrance and clear text matter too. So do a suitable ballot and trained staff. A ballot is what you use to mark your choice. It lets you cast that choice. Public life is more than voting. States must support taking part in public affairs. They must support participation in parties and civic groups. They must support organizations of people with disabilities too. This covers local and national levels. It covers regional and international levels too. A secret vote is not a reason to ban help that someone asks for. The helper should assist the person to cast their own choice. They must not decide it for them. Access and privacy must work together. The goal is a vote people can cast, not one blocked by the process.
